title: Deep-End Blue
passage:
Fill a glass at the pool and the water in it is colorless; fill the pool and it is blue. The sky usually gets the credit and the tiling gets the rest, but the municipal pool at Hallvik settles that question rather neatly: the hall has no windows, the liner is white, and the water is blue anyway. Water absorbs red light a little more readily than blue, and the effect accumulates — undetectable across the width of a glass, obvious across two meters of water, which is why the shallow end is the paler end of the same pool. A white liner adds no color of its own. What it does is send the light back for a second pass, doubling the distance the red has to survive.
— Tova Ingelsson, science desk

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the municipal pool at Hallvik?

options.text: To show that artificial lighting draws out a tint in water that daylight tends to wash away.
To show that a white lining brings out more color in a pool than a blue lining does.
To show that water can look blue where there is no sky to reflect and no colored surface to borrow from.
To show that the blue of a pool comes from what is dissolved in the water rather than from the water itself.

questions.rationale: TYPE-006 purpose item. The pool is introduced immediately after the two popular explanations — 'The sky usually gets the credit and the tiling gets the rest' — and every detail given about it strips one of them away: 'the hall has no windows, the liner is white, and the water is blue anyway'. Its function in the argument is therefore to rule both borrowed sources out, which is what C states. A = outside_knowledge: the windowless hall means the light is artificial, so a reader may promote that incidental fact into the point, but the text never compares artificial light with daylight or claims either brings out a tint. B = surface_word_match with a comparison the text refuses to make: the white liner is discussed, but only as something that 'adds no color of its own' and sends the light back for a second pass; no blue lining is mentioned and no ranking of liners is offered. D = a plausible real-world belief (chemicals or minerals coloring the water) that the passage contradicts, since it attributes the blue to water's own absorption of red light. Note that D would also be the wrong answer to this stem even if it were true, because the Hallvik pool is offered against the sky-and-tiles explanation, not against a chemical one.
